subject: Banking
title: Wirecard: Europe's Enron
description: A short lesson to help you apply Wirecard: Europe's Enron.

hook.text: Wirecard claimed $2.1 billion in bank accounts that didn't exist. Germany's fintech star was a complete fabrication.

buildup.text: Wirecard was a German payment processor worth $28 billion. It joined the DAX 30 index, replacing Commerzbank.

discovery.text: Journalists at the Financial Times found that Wirecard's Asian revenue was fake.

twist.text: German regulators investigated the journalists, not Wirecard.

climax.text: Wirecard showed that regulators can become protectors of fraud.

punchline.text: $2.1 billion that never existed. Regulators attacked the journalists.

quiz.question: What did German regulators do when Wirecard fraud was alleged?
options: Investigated the journalists and banned short-selling Wirecard stock

details.summary: Wirecard, a German payments company, fabricated $2.1 billion in cash that did not exist, fooling auditors, regulators, and investors for years before collapsing in 2020 in Europe's largest corporate fraud since the war.
details.whyItMatters: Wirecard's fraud exposed catastrophic failures in German financial regulation and corporate auditing. The scandal humiliated BaFin, Germany's financial regulator, which had actively protected Wirecard from whistle-blower allegations.
takeaways: $2.1 billion in reported cash balances simply did not exist
Auditor EY failed to verify bank balances for years
Germany's regulator BaFin attacked short sellers instead of investigating

faq.question: How did Wirecard fake $2.1 billion?
faq.answer: Wirecard claimed the cash was held in trustee accounts at Philippine banks. Auditor EY accepted third-party confirmations rather than directly verifying with the banks, which later said no such accounts existed.

faq.question: Why did regulators protect Wirecard instead of investigating?
faq.answer: BaFin viewed Wirecard as a German tech champion and treated short sellers and investigative journalists as market manipulators. The regulator filed criminal complaints against Financial Times reporters who exposed the fraud.
